title: A role for the OsMPK6 signaling pathway in regulating rice grain size
content: Rice (Oryza sativa) serves as a staple food for more than half of the world's population, contributing over 20% of the world's caloric intake. Enhancing rice yield is therefore crucial to ensuring food security, especially in the face of global climate change. Grain size is one of the key agronomic traits that determine crop yield. Organ growth, whether in plants or animals, is a fundamental biological process, governed by cell division and differentiation processes. For instance, do you know why the tomatoes we get in the supermarket are much bigger than their wild varieties? The secret is the FRUIT WEIGHT2.2 (FW2.2) gene. The change in the expression pattern of FW2.2 led to prolonged cell divisions in fruit carpel and thus more cells, resulting in bigger tomatoes (Frary et al. 2000; Cong and Tanksley 2006). In maize, CELL NUMBER REGULATOR genes (ZmCNR1 and 2), which are close homologs of FW2.2, regulate organ size, primarily through cell divisions (Guo et al. 2010). The orthologous rice gene CNR1 determines the grain width and weight through changes in cell number and size (Ruan et al. 2020). Moreover, the OsMKKKK10-OsMKK4-OsMPK6 signaling cascade positively regulates cell proliferation and thus grain size and width (Xu et al. 2018). OsMKKKK10 phosphorylates OsMKK4, which in turn phosphorylates OsMPK6, promoting cell proliferation. Furthermore, recent studies have shown that a GRAS family protein, OsSCL7 (OsGRAS19), negatively regulates grain size (Lin et al. 2019; Zou et al. 2023). However, the exact molecular mechanism of how OsSCL7 regulates grain size has yet to be elucidated.
